name: Nicholas II of Russia
summary: Nicholas II held that the tsar's authority was God-given and absolute, and he refused to share power with elected bodies in his 1895 speech and afterwards. Under pressure from the 1905 revolution he accepted the October Manifesto and a Duma, but he kept his powers and dissolved Dumas that opposed him. He promoted the Hague disarmament conferences, backed Russian expansion in the Far East, and led Russia into the First World War before abdicating in March 1917.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He kept the hereditary imperial throne in the 1906 laws (Article 25).

arms-reduction.rationale: His 1898 rescript proposed an international conference to put an end to the progressive development of armaments.

collective-defense.rationale: He kept the Franco-Russian alliance, concluded as a mutual-defence pact, and Russia entered the First World War alongside its allies.

conscription.rationale: Article 70 declares defence of the throne and fatherland a sacred duty and makes the male population subject to military service.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Article 4 grounds obedience to the Tsar's authority in God's command, not in the consent of the governed.

decide-locally.rationale: His 1899 manifesto abolished Finland's separate constitution and placed its lawmaking under the imperial council, and his government restricted minority self-rule.

democracy-best.rationale: He promulgated a constitution that keeps supreme autocratic power in the Tsar, whose absolute veto and appointment of half the upper house limit any elected body (Articles 4, 9, 100).

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Article 25 makes the imperial throne hereditary in the ruling house.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Article 4 states that obedience to the Tsar's supreme power is commanded by God.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Article 25 makes the throne hereditary in the ruling house, and his abdication manifesto passed the throne within the family.

elective-rulers.rationale: Article 25 makes the throne hereditary and Article 17 has the Tsar himself appoint ministers.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its rationale is about other international bodies (such as the EU, WTO, IMF or WHO) or about support, funding or reform without enforcement powers, and the statement now asks whether the UN should have powers to enforce its decisions against member states.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: His government pursued an institutionalised anti-Semitic policy: quotas for Jews in higher schools, exclusion from law practice, zemstvos and city councils, and persecution of Christian dissenters.

head-commands-forces.rationale: He took personal supreme command of the army in 1915 and kept command of the armed forces as sovereign.

land-redistribution.rationale: Article 77 allows property to be taken for public use with compensation, which fits either answer, and the January 1906 speech the earlier answer rested on could not be opened.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: An archival study reports that he told the German ambassador in 1907 that a world union of Jews and Masons was a deadly danger, and he blamed Jews for the revolution in his letters.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: His 1899 manifesto abolished the Finnish constitution that had been honoured since 1809, and he curtailed minority nationalities' rights.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a monarch who rules, and the statement now asks only about a ceremonial head of state, on which the sources cited here are silent.

more-religion-public.rationale: The 1906 laws make Orthodoxy the ruling faith, name the Tsar defender of its doctrines and have the church administered through the Synod his power created (Articles 62-65).

national-church-status.rationale: Articles 62-65 make Orthodoxy the ruling faith and the Tsar its defender, while other faiths are only tolerated (Article 66).

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: He continued his father's curtailment of minority nationalities' rights and Russification.

national-self-determination.rationale: His 1899 manifesto abolished Finland's constitution, and he carried on his father's curtailment of minority nationalities' rights.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Under Articles 9 and 99 no law exists without his approval and he sets the Duma's sessions, so the Duma is subordinate to the monarch.

participatory-democracy.rationale: His 1895 rejection concerned zemstvo representatives sharing in government, which is not ordinary people's direct part in decisions on their daily lives.

property-fundamental.rationale: Article 77 of the 1906 Fundamental Laws declares property inviolable and allows taking it only for public use with just compensation.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Articles 62-65 make Orthodoxy the ruling faith with the Tsar as its defender, and other faiths only tolerated (Article 66).

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: His government ordered the capture and punishment of all strike leaders in 1897, and a Siberian strike was violently suppressed in 1912.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Article 5 of the 1906 Fundamental Laws, which he issued, declares the person of the Tsar sacred and inviolable.

second-chamber.rationale: The 1906 laws create a Council of the Empire, half appointed by the Tsar, alongside the elected Duma (Article 100).

security-forces-accountable.rationale: He pardoned many convicted pogromists and the Council of Ministers' wish to prosecute the police organiser Podgorichani went nowhere, according to the archival study.

separate-church-state.rationale: Articles 62-65 make Orthodoxy the established faith and have the autocratic power govern the church through the Holy Synod.

separated-powers.rationale: The 1906 laws vest all governmental powers in the Tsar, give him an absolute veto and sole power over ministers (Articles 9, 10, 17).

smash-state-machine.rationale: He signed the October Manifesto that remade the state order and then kept autocratic powers, so the record points both ways and no source settles replacing its institutions.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Article 5 makes his person inviolable and Article 9 lets him alone approve laws, while Article 84 has the empire governed by laws passed by regular procedure.

strong-leader.rationale: The 1906 laws keep supreme autocratic power in the Tsar, with an absolute veto and sole appointment and dismissal of ministers (Articles 4, 9, 17).

suppress-opposition.rationale: He dissolved the first Duma after six weeks, kept up censorship, had strike leaders punished and violently put down strikes, and took a confrontational stance toward the Duma after 1911.

territorial-expansion.rationale: His government pushed Russia into Manchuria and Korea, which led to the war with Japan in 1904.

notes: Later pass bringing the audit up to rules 7 (Claude Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-20). Answers now rest on documents opened in this pass: the 1906 Fundamental Laws he promulgated (his record of autocratic power, veto, hereditary throne, state church, property, conscription), the 1898 Hague rescript, his abdication manifesto, the October Manifesto, his 1914-1917 letters to Alexandra (Pares edition, 30 monthly files read and searched for the Duma, Jews, peace, strikes, church and ministers; they are mostly personal and military and settle few statements), Britannica, the Encyclopedia of Russian History and the Cahiers du monde russe study of his stance on pogroms. Earlier answers resting only on Wikipedia or on pages not reopened were re-sourced or nulled with a reviewHistory entry. The October Manifesto and Stolypin's land reform are treated as not his own position. Themes searched: government, church, economy, war and alliances, minorities, strikes and security; the economy, technology, ecology, gender and most liberty statements have no document by him that settles them.
